Home Nurse

By: Busisiwe Gumede | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
When the serious effects of the covid-19 pandemic set in last year, Mpume Ndabla, a trauma nurse at Netcare quit her job and came up with an initiative that saved many lives

Unique Selling Point:
Amid a global pandemic, when the world needed leadership in healthcare more than ever, registered nurse Mpume Ndabula answered the call and provided home based care to people battling COVID-19. We find out how this young nurse changes lives by bringing ingenuity to the everyday issues impacting her patients and community.

Summary:
Mpumi Ndabula is a registered nurse who provides care to frail and vulnerable COVID-19 patients, all this in the comfort of their own homes surrounded by their loved ones. Ndabula worked as a nurse at Netcare’s trauma and emergency department for 11 years before leaving it all at the height of the first wave last year. She says the psychological impact of her experience as a nurse at that hospital affected her immensely and she felt that the hospital didn’t provide the mental health support that she deserved. What made her situation worse was the long hours waiting for people to die, depression, insomnia and isolation.



Further information:
But there was another reason that compelled her to quit her job. Her mother contracted COVID-19 and was unable to secure a bed at a nearby hospital in roodepoort. Mpumi decided to treat her at home. This meant that she had to buy expensive oxygen machines just to keep her alive. Her mother eventually survived. But this made her realise that there were many other people who needed help taking care of their sick loved ones. She established a home based care initiative, going into people’s homes with a registered doctor, providing healthcare for people who weren’t able to secure beds or weren’t considered “sick enough’ for admission. Mpumi drives to patient’s homes to assess their condition with the help of a doctor as some patient conditions may be outside her scope of work as a nurse. So far she has treated about 30 people in Roodepoort. She has many success stories and one case in which a patient died. That case haunts her because she says she did everything she could to advise the family to seek further medical help from a hospital but the family refused. Even though that was out of her hands she believes that she could have done more for him. Her treatment method comes with the usage of an oxygen machine which costs R9 000,00. Sometimes she uses gas cylinders in the not-so-complicated cases. A cylinder goes for R5 000. It’s difficult to buy these machines because of the high demand due to Coronavirus.

Script:


VO – When the lockdown was announced in March 2020, no one could have predicted the scale in which the country would need all healthcare worker hands on deck to curb the spread of the coronavirus – including those of nurses whose specialty is taking of the injured in casualty wards. Mpumi Ndabula from Alberton in Gauteng is one such registered trauma nurse.
MPUMI NDABULA – NURSE

05:13 - ... we're used to having patients coming in casualties, getting treated and getting moved to the ward or ICU or they get discharged. 05:23 - but with Covid we started having ICU patients spending days in casualty and literally we’d have beds in passages that’s how bad it was.
LINK - When you're a frontline worker faced with overwhelming circumstances - like the kind experienced during a global pandemic - you learn quickly to think on your feet. Just like nurse Mpumi Ndabula who established an initiative of treating patients in the comfort of their own homes.
VO - it was an idea that was inspired by her mother Fikile Ndabula, who contracted COVID-19 in January. Most of them were people who couldn’t get beds in overcrowded hospitals and deserved the type of care she was able to offer her mother.

VO - Fikile’s condition quickly worsened and she was taken to hospital. But Mpumi was concerned that due to patient overcrowding, her mother might not get the best care in hospital. With the family's approval, Mpumi took her mom out of hospital and made it her responsibility to nurse her – at home.
THANDI NDABULA – MPUMI'S MOTHER

02:43 – THANDI - I was facing this sickness even though I didn’t know what it was. 02:28 – ... I felt hot and I was dizzy, the headache was very strong and I didn’t have an appetite. I was very weak.

VO – Staff and PPE shortages meant that nurses were overworked and ill-equipped in the face of a deadly, unfamiliar virus. VO – Mpumi also felt the pressure during the pandemic. She resigned from her post at a private hospital to focus on her wellbeing.
MPUMI NDABULA – NURSE

people were dying and nobody asked how the nurses were doing.

MPUMI NDABULA – NURSE

09:54 - … … after nursing other patients who were in the hospital and losing a lot of the patients as well for me emotionally that was just a lot and I needed some time to find myself.
VO – People with mild covid symptoms were urged to self-isolate in their homes. This somewhat helped to ease the pressure on South Africa's overburdened healthcare system but it meant that many patients embarked on treatment regimens without the benefit of frequent intervention by a healthcare professional – a scary prospect.

Providing home-based care for her mother was an obvious decision for Mpumi even if it exposed her to the risk of also contracting the virus.
MPUMI NDABULA – NURSE

14:35 - ... I started thinking about a treatment plan and what we are going to do when we take her out of the hospital.
VO – Getting a reliable oxygen source was the priority. The hefty price tag is around R9 000 for an oxygen machine and R5 000 for a cylinder. At first, Mpumi could only afford to hire the contraption.
MPUMI NDABULA – NURSE

18:19 - This one time we ran out of oxygen and we had to go refill it. So we went to the pharmacy and the long queue that I found there it was so traumatising. 18:30 - ... I said to this guy... 18:42 - My mom is very sick she needs oxygen. And they looked at me and said “no, all these people need oxygen.”
VO – Thandi saw that the cost of her treatment weighed heavily on her daughter.
THANDI NDABULA – MPUMI'S MOTHER

12:56 - First day she hired the machine it was about R1400, so to refill it it would take about an hour . So she would take two bottles - and she ended up buying the big machine because she saw that she spent a lot.
VO – Despite the challenges, Thandi had faith in her daughter's ability as a nurse. Mpumi, on the other hand, was nervous.
MPUMI NDABULA – NURSE

19: 06 – CLAIRE - How did you separate daughter and nurse responsibilities while you’re looking after your mother who is also now your critical patient?

18:13 – MPUMI -It was not easy because it was like, she is a patient but she is not a patient. This is my mother we are talking about. 19:31 - It was tough every day for me I had to be nursing her while I was crying.
VO – Thankfully, Thandi's condition improved and weeks later, she was cleared of the virus.


VO – Mpumi was so relieved that her gamble paid off, she shared the great news online. She didn't expect that her experience would open a new door in her career path – home-based care.
MPUMI NDABULA – NURSE

21:48 - ... I posted about my mother on Twitter about how I helped her and it became a huge thing that Sunday. Everybody was like 'oh my gosh, this is so amazing. Can you come and help?”
VO – Mpumi would soon put her cylinders to good use.


One of the first people to reach out to Mpumi on social media was Joan von Meyer from Kempton Park, in Gauteng's east rand.
LINK - Even though his condition was worsening, Mr Von Meyer’s wife Joan took the risky decision to choose home based care over an overcrowded hospital. It was a gamble that ended up paying off.
VO – Joan's husband, Graeme von Meyer, was admitted into hospital just days before Mpumi posted about her mother's treatment journey on Twitter.
JOAN VON MEYER – PATIENT'S WIFE

02:16 – JOAN - ... I have never seen so many people, a lot of people that were sick and on oxygen all at the same time. It was, for me personally, it overwhelmed me.


VO – Graeme says the hospital he was in had enough beds
Greame VON MEYER – PATIENT

04:05 - ... in a space where they would have four beds, you find there is ten people.. 08:10 - … we decided that it would be best that we get the nurse to come and treat me on a one-on-one basis so that my chances of recovery could be better.
VO - Joan was delighted when Mpumi took her call.Mpumi's treatment approach went beyond just administering medicine and oxygen. She worked alongside a doctor, making sure patients receive the best care.









VO –
Greame VON MEYER – PATIENT

16:42 - Nurse Mpume was able to show my wife and daughter how I must do my breathing exercises. So during the course of the day daughter and I would be on our backs with our legs up counting through the breathing exercises and she would walk me around the yard and to the gate.
VO – With each exercise session, Graeme regained his strength.
Greame VON MEYER – PATIENT

10:58 - It took me at least about 10 days for the medication to start working and initially a person is so weak that you can’t even walk.
VO – He has recovered but is still waiting on his senses to return to normal.
Greame VON MEYER – PATIENT

14:13 - ... The taste and smell is not back a 100% so sometimes when the wife is cooking you can’t get any smell, which is bad because she is a good cook.
LINK - The COVID-19 pandemic has proven to the world what we already know; that nursing is a calling - not a job. And that is the sentiment shared by many people who have witnessed the love and care of nurse Mpumi Ndabula.
VO – To date, Mpumi has treated about thirty patients
MPUMI NDABULA – NURSE

23:41 - ... I know what it’s like when you need help and you're all on your own and don’t know what to do. 23:52 - So I was like, I have to go there it doesn’t matter whether I’m from work and tired. Let me just go and help out these people

VO – The von Meyers say no words can ever adequately express their gratitude to Mpumi for providing quality care in their time of need, even if meant putting her own life at risk.
JOAN VON MEYER – PATIENT'S WIFE

13:30 - We are happy to have known Nurse Mpumi. 11:02 - … she’s very soft spoken… she is very loving. She’s so heartwarming.
Greame VON MEYER – PATIENT

12:42 - ... It was the best care that I could have got. 13:22 - ... she is part of the family now. Not only is she on speed dial. When we needed advice for a family friend that also contracted COVID she was available
